title: With `min.insync.replicas=1`, `acks=all`, replication factor 3 — where is the actual durability risk?
shortTitle: With min.insync.replicas=1, acks=all, replication factor 3 — where is the actual durability risk?

s1_definition.profdef: The setting `acks=all` tells the producer to wait until all in-sync replicas have acknowledged a write, and `min.insync.replicas` defines how many replicas must be in-sync for that write to be accepted at all. With replication factor three but `min.insync.replicas=1`, the "all" in `acks=all` can legally mean "just the one replica that is currently in-sync," namely the leader alone. The durability risk is that during a period when followers have fallen out of the in-sync replica set, a message can be acknowledged as durable while existing on only a single broker; if that broker's disk is lost before any follower catches up, the acknowledged message is gone forever.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India promises that a transfer record is safe only once three separate vaults each hold a copy. Here the policy says you keep three vaults, and you always wait for "all currently open vaults" to confirm, but you also allow the bank to keep operating with as few as one open vault. One afternoon two vault doors jam shut, leaving only the head vault open. A clerk records Rajesh's transfer, the head vault confirms, and the bank tells Rajesh "safely stored in all open vaults." But "all open vaults" was just one vault. That night the head vault floods and its records are destroyed before the other two vaults reopened and copied the record. Rajesh's transfer is gone, even though the bank had promised it was safe.
s1_definition.oneliner: With `min.insync.replicas=1`, `acks=all` degrades to "acknowledged by the leader alone" whenever followers are out of sync, so a single broker or disk failure can lose an already-acknowledged write — set `min.insync.replicas=2` with replication factor three to get real durability.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The setting `acks=all` tells the producer to wait until all in-sync replicas have acknowledged a write, and `min.insync.replicas` defines how many replicas must be in-sync for that write to be accepted at all. With replication factor three but `min.insync.replicas=1`, the "all" in `acks=all` can legally mean "just the one replica that is currently in-sync," namely the leader alone. The durability risk is that during a period when followers have fallen out of the in-sync replica set, a message can be acknowledged as durable while existing on only a single broker; if that broker's disk is lost before any follower catches up, the acknowledged message is gone forever.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India promises that a transfer record is safe only once three separate vaults each hold a copy. Here the policy says you keep three vaults, and you always wait for "all currently open vaults" to confirm, but you also allow the bank to keep operating with as few as one open vault. One afternoon two vault doors jam shut, leaving only the head vault open. A clerk records Rajesh's transfer, the head vault confirms, and the bank tells Rajesh "safely stored in all open vaults." But "all open vaults" was just one vault. That night the head vault floods and its records are destroyed before the other two vaults reopened and copied the record. Rajesh's transfer is gone, even though the bank had promised it was safe.

**One line to remember:** With `min.insync.replicas=1`, `acks=all` degrades to "acknowledged by the leader alone" whenever followers are out of sync, so a single broker or disk failure can lose an already-acknowledged write — set `min.insync.replicas=2` with replication factor three to get real durability.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with what `acks=all` actually promises. It does not mean all replicas; it means all replicas that are currently in the in-sync replica set, often abbreviated ISR. A follower is in the ISR only while it keeps up with the leader within `replica.lag.time.max.ms`. If a follower is slow, is restarting, is doing garbage collection, or is on a broker that is overloaded, it drops out of the ISR. So the ISR can shrink from three down to two or even one at runtime, and `acks=all` adapts to whatever the ISR currently is.

Now bring in `min.insync.replicas`. This is the floor: the leader will only accept a produce request with `acks=all` if the ISR size is at least this number. When you set it to one, the floor is the leader by itself. So the dangerous window is this: two followers have fallen out of the ISR for any reason, the ISR is now just the leader, `min.insync.replicas=1` is satisfied, and the producer's `acks=all` is satisfied by the leader alone. The producer gets a success acknowledgment for a message that physically exists on exactly one broker. If that broker crashes and its disk is unrecoverable before a follower rejoins the ISR and replicates the message, the message is permanently lost, and the producer has no idea because it already got a success.

The fix is to raise the floor. With replication factor three, you set `min.insync.replicas=2`. Now the leader refuses to accept an `acks=all` write unless at least two replicas are in-sync, which guarantees every acknowledged message lives on at least two brokers. If a second replica is not available, the producer gets a `NotEnoughReplicasException` and must retry, so you trade a little availability for the durability guarantee you actually wanted. This is the standard production configuration: replication factor three, `min.insync.replicas=2`, `acks=all`. It tolerates the loss of any one broker without losing acknowledged data, while still accepting writes.

A critical nuance is that durability requires all three settings to agree. Replication factor three alone does nothing if `acks` is not `all`, because with `acks=1` the producer is acknowledged as soon as the leader writes, regardless of followers. And `acks=all` alone is not enough if `min.insync.replicas=1`, as explained. The three settings are a contract and only the combination of replication factor three, `acks=all`, and `min.insync.replicas=2` gives the guarantee. In code the producer side is simply:

```java
props.put(ProducerConfig.ACKS_CONFIG, "all");
props.put(ProducerConfig.ENABLE_IDEMPOTENCE_CONFIG, true); // avoid dup on retry
props.put(ProducerConfig.RETRIES_CONFIG, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
props.put(ProducerConfig.DELIVERY_TIMEOUT_MS_CONFIG, 120000);
```

and the topic side carries the real durability knob:

```bash
kafka-topics.sh --alter --topic settlements \
  --config min.insync.replicas=2 --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092
```

Further senior-level points: `min.insync.replicas` is enforced per partition, so the risk is evaluated partition by partition, and a topic can have some healthy partitions and some at-risk partitions simultaneously. You should alert on the metric that exposes under-replicated or at-minimum-ISR partitions, because a partition sitting at ISR equal to one is a silent durability hole even while everything looks green. There is also the related `unclean.leader.election.enable` setting: if that is true, a broker that was not in the ISR can be elected leader after a failure, which trades consistency for availability and can also lose acknowledged data; for a bank you keep it false. Finally, remember that even replication factor three with `min.insync.replicas=2` is not immune to a correlated failure such as losing two brokers in the same rack or availability zone at once, which is why you spread replicas across racks or zones using rack awareness.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India writes every settled transfer to the `settlements` topic with replication factor three. During an incident review we discovered the topic had been created with `min.insync.replicas=1` to "keep accepting writes during maintenance."

Problem 1 — on a busy evening, two of the three brokers for a partition were under heavy load and their follower replicas lagged out of the ISR. The ISR for that partition shrank to just the leader. This is the dangerous window: `min.insync.replicas=1` let the leader keep accepting `acks=all` writes alone.

Problem 2 — Rajesh's settlement was acknowledged as successful while it existed only on the leader broker. Minutes later that broker suffered a disk failure before any follower rejoined and copied the data. The settlement was lost, yet the producer had received a success. This is exactly the acknowledged-but-single-copy durability risk.

Our runnable demo models a `PartitionReplication` object with a leader and two followers, an ISR set that can shrink, and a `DurabilityPolicy` that enforces `min.insync.replicas`. We produce one message under `minIsr=1` with a degraded ISR, then kill the leader and show the message is lost; then we repeat under `minIsr=2` and show the write is rejected rather than falsely acknowledged, so nothing is ever lost. The classes are `DurabilityDemo`, `PartitionReplication`, `DurabilityPolicy`, and `NotEnoughReplicasException`.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: kafka-1:9092,kafka-2:9092,kafka-3:9092
    producer:
      acks: all                       # wait for ALL in-sync replicas
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true
        retries: 2147483647
        delivery.timeout.ms: 120000
# Topic durability is set on the topic, not the producer:
#   replication.factor = 3
#   min.insync.replicas = 2   <-- the real durability floor
#   unclean.leader.election.enable = false
```

```bash

mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run it
java -jar target/settlement-durability-service-1.0.0.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod

kafka-topics.sh --alter --topic settlements \
  --config min.insync.replicas=2 --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092

# Run the demo (Case A loses data, Case B refuses to lie)
javac demo/DurabilityDemo.java -d out
java -cp out com.bank.settlement.demo.DurabilityDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a partition with replication factor three on broker-1 (leader), broker-2, and broker-3, and one settlement message for Rajesh, under two configurations.

Step 1 (Case A, minIsr=1): Under load, the followers on broker-2 and broker-3 lag beyond the allowed time and drop out of the ISR. The ISR for this partition is now just broker-1.

Step 2 (Case A): The producer sends Rajesh's settlement with acks=all. The policy checks the ISR size against min.insync.replicas of one; one is at least one, so the write is accepted. The leader appends the record, and because the ISR is just the leader, the record exists on only one broker.

Step 3 (Case A): The producer receives a success acknowledgment. The application believes the settlement is durable. In reality it lives on a single disk.

Step 4 (Case A): Broker-1's disk fails before broker-2 or broker-3 rejoin the ISR and replicate the record. The acknowledged settlement is permanently lost, and nothing in the producer ever reported a problem.

Step 5 (Case B, minIsr=2): Same degraded ISR of just broker-1. The producer sends the same settlement. The policy checks the ISR size of one against min.insync.replicas of two and refuses the write with NotEnoughReplicas. The producer gets an honest failure and will retry once a second replica is back, so no acknowledged message ever exists on a single broker, and nothing is lost.

Final output:

```
[2026-10-24 22:15:40] [INFO] === Case A: min.insync.replicas = 1 (DANGEROUS) ===
[2026-10-24 22:15:40] [INFO] Leader appended message; ISR size = 1
[2026-10-24 22:15:40] [WARNING] Producer received SUCCESS (acks=all satisfied by leader alone)
[2026-10-24 22:15:40] [SEVERE] LEADER DISK LOST — acknowledged message 'Rajesh SAV2001 settle 50000' existed only on the leader and is NOW PERMANENTLY GONE
[2026-10-24 22:15:40] [INFO] === Case B: min.insync.replicas = 2 (SAFE) ===
[2026-10-24 22:15:40] [INFO] Write correctly REJECTED (ISR=1 < minIsr=2): ISR=1 < min.insync.replicas=2 -> no false acknowledgment, no data loss
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The setting acks=all is often misread as "all replicas," but it really means all replicas that are currently in the in-sync set. And min.insync.replicas is the floor for how small that in-sync set is allowed to be while still accepting writes. So the actual durability risk in the configuration of replication factor three, acks=all, and min.insync.replicas one is this: followers can drop out of the in-sync set at runtime because of load, garbage collection, restarts, or slow disks, and when they do, the in-sync set can shrink to just the leader. At that moment min.insync.replicas of one is satisfied and acks=all is satisfied by the leader alone, so the producer gets a success acknowledgment for a message that physically lives on only one broker. If that broker's disk is lost before a follower rejoins and replicates, the acknowledged message is gone, and the producer never learns it failed.

The fix is to raise the floor. With replication factor three you set min.insync.replicas to two. Now the leader refuses any acks=all write unless at least two replicas are in-sync, which guarantees every acknowledged message exists on at least two brokers and survives the loss of any single broker. If a second replica is not available, the producer gets a NotEnoughReplicas error and retries, so you accept a small loss of availability in exchange for the durability you actually wanted.

On the National Bank of India settlement service we learned this the hard way during an incident review: a topic had been created with min.insync.replicas of one to keep accepting writes during maintenance, and under load the in-sync set for a partition shrank to a single broker. A settlement was acknowledged while it lived on one disk, that disk failed, and the settlement was lost even though the producer had reported success. We changed the topic to min.insync.replicas of two, kept acks=all and idempotence on the producer, disabled unclean leader election so a stale replica can never be elected and silently drop data, and spread replicas across racks for availability-zone safety.

The principle I stress to the team is that durability is a contract among three settings, not any one of them. Replication factor three gives you the copies, acks=all makes the producer wait for the in-sync replicas, and min.insync.replicas of two guarantees that "the in-sync replicas" is never just one broker. Miss any one of the three and you have a silent durability hole, which is exactly why I also alert on the under-minimum-in-sync partition metric, because a partition sitting at an in-sync count of one looks perfectly healthy on a dashboard right up until the moment it loses someone's money.

---

keyPoints: Replication factor: copies of each partition across brokers
ISR (In-Sync Replicas): followers caught up with leader
acks=all: wait for all ISR to acknowledge — strongest durability
